text: A case note is the written record of what an analyst did with an alert, and it has one job: let someone else -- another analyst, an auditor, a future version of the same analyst months later -- understand the case completely without redoing the work the first time around.

A real case note covers five things every time: what happened, a plain-language summary of the alert and the activity behind it; what was checked, the specific logs, systems, or accounts reviewed; what was found, the actual results, not just "looks fine"; what action was taken, closed, escalated, or contained; and timestamps for when each of those steps occurred. Leave even one of these out and the note stops doing its job.

"Looked into it, seems fine" is the most common bad case note, and it's worse than writing nothing. It creates the appearance that due diligence happened without recording any of it, so the next person has to start from zero, and an auditor reviewing it later has no way to tell whether anything was actually checked.

Compare that to a clear note on the same alert: timestamped entries showing the raw auth log was checked, the login matched an approved travel ticket, no other accounts were affected, and the ticket closed as a benign true positive. Same outcome, same closed ticket -- only one of these notes actually proves the work happened.

Case notes get read far more often than new analysts expect, and almost never by the person who wrote them in the moment they were written. Tier 2 reads them during an escalation, a different analyst reads them months later when the same account alerts again, an auditor reads them during an incident review or compliance check. Next, Lesson 20 covers escalating to Tier 2 -- and a clear case note is exactly what makes that handoff clean.
